title: Conservatives Report, but Liberals Display, Greater Happiness
note: The researchers compared self-reports with indicators such as smile coding and word choice from other datasets. The political direction of the difference reversed across kinds of measures.

headline: Do cognitive test scores correlate with sperm count or motility?
title: Intelligence and Semen Quality Are Positively Correlated
note: The authors combined cognitive scores and related them to semen measures from a sample of veterans, interpreting positive associations as consistent with shared influences on bodily and cognitive functioning.

headline: Can the width-to-height ratio of hockey players’ faces predict penalty minutes?
title: In Your Face: Facial Metrics Predict Aggressive Behaviour in the Laboratory and in Varsity and Professional Hockey Players
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The authors related face measurements to penalty minutes and separately to responses on a laboratory task, interpreting the associations as evidence that facial shape predicts aggression.

headline: Can the proportions of a man’s face predict whether he lies during a negotiation game?
title: Bad to the Bone: Facial Structure Predicts Unethical Behaviour
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The researchers modeled deception in a negotiation and cheating in a game using men’s facial width-to-height ratio, reporting positive associations.

headline: Do people who click immediately as friends smell more alike?
title: There Is Chemistry in Social Chemistry
note: An electronic nose measured similarity in body odor among established pairs, and a separate experiment related odor similarity to strangers’ reported connection after a nonverbal interaction.

headline: Do people prefer the smell of shirts worn by someone with dissimilar immune-system genes?
title: MHC-Dependent Mate Preferences in Humans
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: Participants rated odors from worn T-shirts. The authors compared ratings across genetic similarity and contraceptive-use groups and interpreted the differences in terms of mate preference.

headline: Can positive words in a nun’s autobiography predict how long she lives?
title: Positive Emotions in Early Life and Longevity: Findings From the Nun Study
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Researchers coded emotional content in short autobiographies written early in adulthood and related the scores to survival decades later.

headline: Will people press a shock button when left alone with their thoughts?
title: Just Think: The Challenges of the Disengaged Mind
note: Across studies, the authors compared enjoyment of thinking with other activities. In one small session, some participants who had rated a shock as unpleasant administered at least one to themselves.

headline: Can touching a teddy bear make excluded adults give more money to someone else?
title: Touching a Teddy Bear Mitigates Negative Effects of Social Exclusion to Increase Prosocial Behavior
note: The researchers compared prosocial outcomes after exclusion with and without touching a teddy bear and interpreted the interaction as mitigation of the effects of exclusion.

headline: Do people approaching a new decade of age behave differently at 29, 39 or 49?
title: People Search for Meaning When They Approach a New Decade in Chronological Age
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared ages ending in nine with neighboring ages across surveys and archival measures such as first-time marathon running. They interpreted the patterns as a search for meaning.

headline: Can reading an argument against free will make people cheat on a later task?
title: The Value of Believing in Free Will: Encouraging a Belief in Determinism Increases Cheating
note: The authors compared cheating proxies after reading passages differing in their treatment of free will or after related belief manipulations. They interpreted the contrasts as effects of weakening belief in free will.

headline: Can describing the same golf task as measuring intelligence or athletic ability reverse a group performance gap?
title: Stereotype Threat Effects on Black and White Athletic Performance
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared golf scores by participant race and how the task was described. They interpreted the interaction as consistent with threat from different stereotypes.

headline: Will children wait longer for a second marshmallow after an adult keeps an unrelated promise?
title: Rational Snacking: Young Children’s Decision-Making on the Marshmallow Task Is Moderated by Beliefs About Environmental Reliability
note: Before the marshmallow task, the experimenter kept or broke promises regarding other materials. The authors compared waiting times and interpreted the difference as evidence that the task also measures expectations about reliability.

headline: Can silhouettes colored in by participants distinguish pride from shame or fear?
title: Bodily Maps of Emotions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants marked where they felt more or less bodily activity on silhouettes. The authors statistically compared the self-reported maps across emotion categories and language groups.

headline: Can a radiologist look straight at a gorilla in a scan and miss it?
title: The Invisible Gorilla Strikes Again: Sustained Inattentional Blindness in Expert Observers
note: While 24 radiologists searched lung CT scans for nodules, 20 missed an inserted gorilla. Eye tracking showed that several who missed it had looked at its location.

headline: Can a cold room make people more inclined to choose a romance movie?
title: Warm It Up With Love: The Effect of Physical Coldness on Liking of Romance Movies
note: Experiments compared genre preferences under cold and warmer conditions. The authors also analyzed rental and temperature records, interpreting the results as a link between physical and psychological warmth.

headline: Can scores on mental-state attribution measures help explain who believes in a personal God?
title: Mentalizing Deficits Constrain Belief in a Personal God
note: The authors analyzed questionnaire data and group differences, then fitted mediation models linking measures of mentalizing to reported belief in a personal God.

headline: Can putting people under stress make them knock on wood more often?
title: The Effects of Stress and Desire for Control on Superstitious Behavior
note: The researchers counted knocking on wood in conditions with different stress levels and examined how the difference depended on participants’ desire for control.

headline: Does the effect of a sugary drink on task performance depend on what you believe about willpower?
title: Beliefs About Willpower Determine the Impact of Glucose on Self-Control
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared self-control task scores by drink condition and by whether participants held or were led to adopt a limited-resource view of willpower.

headline: Can drinking sugary lemonade make someone better at ignoring an irrelevant option?
title: Toward a Physiology of Dual-Process Reasoning and Judgment: Lemonade, Willpower, and Expensive Rule-Based Analysis
note: After a self-control task, participants drank sweetened or artificially sweetened lemonade. Choice rates involving a decoy option were used to infer changes in rule-based reasoning.

headline: Can a reminder of God make people more willing to take a physical risk?
title: Anticipating Divine Protection? Reminders of God Can Increase Nonmoral Risk Taking
note: The authors compared reported or observed risk choices following God-related or neutral cues. They interpreted some differences as expectations of protection and distinguished risks with and without moral implications.

headline: Can reminders of God make people resist cookies but do less work toward a goal?
title: Divergent Effects of Activating Thoughts of God on Self-Regulation
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Different experiments compared temptation resistance and active goal pursuit after God-related cues. The authors reported effects in opposite directions across these outcomes.

headline: Can knocking away from yourself make bad luck feel less likely?
title: Reversing One’s Fortune by Pushing Away Bad Luck
note: After participants made a tempting-fate statement, the authors compared likelihood judgments under actions directed away from or toward the body.

topic: Control and belief in external systems
headline: Can recalling a loss of control make people report stronger belief in a controlling God?
title: God and the Government: Testing a Compensatory Control Mechanism for the Support of External Systems
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared support for external systems under different personal-control conditions and interpreted some changes in belief or endorsement as compensatory.

headline: Can calling the same odor “body odor” instead of “cheddar cheese” change how it smells?
title: Cognitive Modulation of Olfactory Processing
note: The same odor received different pleasantness ratings across labels. The authors also compared fMRI signals and related some differences to those ratings.

headline: Can rinsing your mouth with carbohydrates affect a self-control task without swallowing?
title: Motivational Versus Metabolic Effects of Carbohydrates on Self-Control
note: The researchers compared subsequent task performance after carbohydrate and control rinses. They interpreted the contrast as evidence for a motivational response to oral carbohydrate cues.

headline: Do people report more pain relief from the same placebo if told it costs more?
title: Commercial Features of Placebo and Therapeutic Efficacy
note: Participants received an identical placebo labeled with different prices. The investigators compared changes in ratings of experimentally induced pain.

headline: Are people talking on phones less likely to notice a clown riding a unicycle?
title: Did You See the Unicycling Clown? Inattentional Blindness While Walking and Talking on a Cell Phone
note: The field study compared how often pedestrians in different walking and phone-use conditions reported noticing the same conspicuous event.

headline: Can a hypnotic suggestion to see gray alter brain responses to a colored image?
title: Hypnotic Visual Illusion Alters Color Processing in the Brain
note: Researchers compared imaging signals under color and grayscale suggestions in highly hypnotizable participants, including when the physical stimulus conflicted with the suggestion.

headline: Can altered video make someone confess to breaking a rule they did not actually break?
title: Innocent but Proven Guilty: Eliciting Internalized False Confessions Using Doctored-Video Evidence
note: The authors compared confessions and belief in the alleged rule violation across types of purported video evidence.

headline: Can a doctored childhood photo make someone describe a balloon ride that never happened?
title: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Lies: Using False Photographs to Create False Childhood Memories
note: After viewing edited childhood photos and being interviewed, some participants gave accounts of the fictitious balloon ride. Researchers coded these accounts for recalled details.

headline: Can reading a trolley problem in a foreign language change willingness to push someone off a bridge?
title: Your Morals Depend on Language
note: The authors compared hypothetical answers across native- and foreign-language conditions. The reported shift was concentrated in the version requiring direct physical harm.

headline: Do intoxicated participants find more solutions to puzzles that link three unrelated words?
title: Uncorking the Muse: Alcohol Intoxication Facilitates Creative Problem Solving
note: The authors compared scores and response times on a word-association task across intoxicated and sober groups and interpreted the result in terms of creative problem solving.

headline: Can simply expecting to interact with a woman lower men’s scores on an attention task?
title: The Mere Anticipation of an Interaction With a Woman Can Impair Men’s Cognitive Performance
note: The researchers compared cognitive task scores when participants believed another person was observing them or would interact with them. They interpreted some differences among men as an effect of anticipated opposite-sex interaction.

headline: Do men score lower on a cognitive task after a short conversation with a woman?
title: Interacting With Women Can Impair Men’s Cognitive Functioning
note: The authors compared task performance after different social interactions and examined whether men’s scores varied with their ratings of the interaction partner.

headline: Can making a person’s hand look larger change the temperature at which stimulation feels painful?
title: Visual Distortion of Body Size Modulates Pain Perception
note: Participants viewed magnified, reduced or unaltered images of their hands during a thermal task. The authors compared the temperatures at which participants first reported pain.

headline: Does looking at your own hand change how painful the same laser pulse feels?
title: Visually Induced Analgesia: Seeing the Body Reduces Pain
note: The researchers compared pain ratings and brain responses to calibrated laser stimulation while participants looked at their own hand or an object.

headline: Can someone show a facial reaction to an emotional image they report not seeing?
title: Unseen Facial and Bodily Expressions Trigger Fast Emotional Reactions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In people with visual-field loss, the researchers compared facial muscle and pupil responses to expressions shown in seen and unseen areas of the visual field.

headline: Same photo, red background. More attractive?
title: Romantic Red: Red Enhances Men's Attraction to Women
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Researchers changed the colors surrounding photos or the colors of women's clothing and asked men to rate attractiveness. The authors reported higher ratings in several of the red conditions.

headline: Does typing your notes make you learn less?
title: The pen is mightier than the keyboard: advantages of longhand over laptop note taking
note: The authors reported that laptop note takers performed worse on conceptual questions than longhand note takers in their lecture experiments.

headline: Can writing about a time you were in charge change whether you would fire someone?
title: From Power to Inaction: Ambivalence Gives Pause to the Powerful
note: In one experiment, participants wrote about a time they had high or low power, then decided whether they would fire a hypothetical employee. The study reported an interaction between felt power and ambivalence. A student replication did not reproduce the interaction. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1177/0956797616669947/

headline: Can a background question change someone’s math score?
title: Stereotype Susceptibility: Identity Salience and Shifts in Quantitative Performance
note: The authors reported different math scores among Asian American women depending on whether preceding questions cued ethnicity or gender. A larger replication recovered the predicted pattern after excluding participants unfamiliar with the relevant stereotypes. The full sample did not show the effect. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000184

headline: Are men more attractive to women when shown in red?
title: Red, rank, and romance in women viewing men
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Will a woman choose a red shirt to meet an attractive man?
title: Women's use of red clothing as a sexual signal in intersexual interaction
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does the red-attraction effect extend across cultures?
title: Red enhances women's attractiveness to men: First evidence suggesting universality
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does a red shirt change how men approach women?
title: Red and romantic behavior in men viewing women
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can French accordion music tilt a supermarket’s wine sales toward French bottles?
title: The influence of in-store music on wine selections
note: A supermarket alternated French and German music near wines from both countries. Sales shifted toward the wine whose country matched the music, while shoppers generally did not report that the music had influenced their choice.

headline: Can a drink’s color override what people say they know about its flavor?
title: The influence of color-generated expectations on the identification of flavored drinks
note: Adding a color associated with a particular flavor increased flavor-identification responses matching that expectation, even when participants were told color was uninformative. The effect weakened when the drink’s actual flavor strongly conflicted with the color cue.

headline: Can an unpleasant smell alter how people learn from social feedback?
title: Aversive smell associations shape social judgment
note: The study paired social information with an aversive odor and examined how participants later evaluated people. The authors reported that odor-associated learning changed subsequent social judgments.

headline: Can observers guess fertility from how a woman walks?
title: Gait and menstrual cycle: Ovulating women use sexier gaits and walk slowly ahead of men
note: Researchers secretly recorded women walking ahead of a male confederate and compared gait across cycle phases. The authors reported that gait ratings changed near ovulation, interpreting the pattern as a possible attractiveness cue.

headline: Do women report feeling more attractive around ovulation?
title: Self-perceived and observed variations in women’s attractiveness throughout the menstrual cycle—a diary study
note: In a daily diary study following women through a menstrual cycle, researchers tracked self-rated attractiveness and clothing. They reported cycle-linked variation in how attractive participants felt and in how others rated their appearance.

headline: Do clothing choices shift with the menstrual cycle?
title: Changes in women’s choice of dress across the ovulatory cycle: Naturalistic and laboratory task-based evidence
note: Across a naturalistic study and a laboratory choice task, the paper reported that women’s clothing choices became more revealing or sexy near the fertile phase, with differences depending on relationship and individual characteristics.

headline: Does relationship status change which male body odor women prefer near ovulation?
title: Women’s preference for dominant male odour: Effects of menstrual cycle and relationship status
note: Women rated male body odors, and the study compared odor preferences across menstrual-cycle phases and relationship status. The authors reported stronger fertile-phase preference for odors from men scoring higher on a dominance questionnaire, particularly among partnered women.

headline: When asked who is more likely to commit an extreme crime, do people pick atheists?
title: Everything Is Permitted? People Intuitively Judge Immorality as Representative of Atheists
note: Across five experiments, participants matched highly immoral acts—including serial murder and consensual incest—to social groups. The authors reported that even atheist participants were more likely to associate the acts with atheists than with other religious or cultural groups.

headline: Do pictures of eyes increase real-world donations more than pictures of noses or mouths?
title: Eyes, More Than Other Facial Features, Enhance Real-World Donation Behavior
note: Researchers alternated donation signs featuring eyes, noses, mouths, or chairs. They reported higher donations when eyes were displayed than when the other facial features or chairs were shown.

headline: Are shoppers more likely to help a stranger when the mall smells like baking cookies?
title: The Sweet Smell of... Helping: Effects of Pleasant Ambient Fragrance on Prosocial Behavior in Shopping Malls
note: In two shopping-mall field studies, passersby encountered a dropped-pen or change-making request near pleasant odors such as baking cookies or roasting coffee. The paper reported higher helping rates when pleasant fragrances were present.

headline: Does chocolate taste better when someone else tastes it at the same time?
title: Shared Experiences Are Amplified
note: In experiments, participants tasted chocolate or listened to music while another person either shared the experience at the same time or did a different task. The authors reported that pleasant and unpleasant experiences felt more intense when shared, even without talking.

headline: Can a brief touch on the arm increase how much money people sacrifice for a stranger?
title: Monetary sacrifice among strangers is mediated by endogenous oxytocin release after physical contact
note: In a monetary contribution experiment, physical contact followed by an intentional act of trust was reported to raise oxytocin and increase monetary sacrifice to a stranger by 243% relative to untouched controls.

headline: Do photographs of tearful people make strangers more willing to help?
title: The social impact of emotional tears
note: Across two studies, participants viewed images of people crying or not crying and reported willingness to help. The authors reported that tears increased helping intentions, with perceived helplessness and felt connection accounting for part of the difference.

headline: Can seeing an unfamiliar shape make you like it even when you cannot recognize it?
title: The Mere Exposure Effect Is Differentially Sensitive to Different Judgment Tasks
note: Participants saw random shapes so briefly that recognition was at chance in one experiment; repeated shapes were still judged more positively and brighter.

headline: Can an entire person change during a conversation without being noticed?
title: Failure to Detect Changes to People During a Real-World Interaction
note: During a staged conversation, a brief interruption allowed one person to be replaced by another. Many participants did not notice the change.

headline: Does knowing that a computer saved a fact make people forget the fact itself?
title: Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips
note: Participants remembered less information when they expected it to remain available on a computer, while better remembering where it had been stored.

headline: Can changing only the uniform color change a referee’s score?
title: When the Referee Sees Red…
note: Taekwondo referees scored videos whose uniform colors were digitally swapped. The authors reported more points for the same contestant when shown in red.

headline: Can being unsure whether someone likes you make them more attractive?
title: “He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not…”: Uncertainty Can Increase Romantic Attraction
note: Women shown men's Facebook profiles reported the most attraction when told it was uncertain how much the men liked them.

headline: Does beer taste worse if you hear about the vinegar before drinking it?
title: Try It, You’ll Like It: The Influence of Expectation, Consumption, and Revelation on Preferences for Beer
note: Telling drinkers about the balsamic vinegar before tasting reduced their preference for the doctored beer; telling them afterward did not have the same effect.

headline: Do preverbal babies choose a puppet that helped another puppet climb a hill?
title: Social Evaluation by Preverbal Infants
note: Infants watched characters help or hinder another character going uphill. The authors reported that infants reaching for a character favored the helper.

headline: Can turning up bar music make people drink beer faster?
title: Sound Level of Environmental Music and Drinking Behavior: A Field Experiment With Beer Drinkers
note: In two bars, the authors reported faster beer drinking and higher consumption during louder music than during normal-volume music.

headline: Does a printed joke with the bill make diners tip more?
title: The Effects of a Joke on Tipping When It Is Delivered at the Same Time as the Bill
note: In a field experiment, the authors reported larger gratuities when a joke accompanied the bill than when it did not.

headline: Can thinking about death make people expect to spend more or take more from a shared resource?
title: Of Wealth and Death: Materialism, Mortality Salience, and Consumption Behavior
note: People reminded of their mortality projected more spending and, in a separate resource game, took more for themselves.

headline: Can putting your feet on someone’s desk make you look more powerful?
title: Breaking the Rules to Rise to Power: How Norm Violators Gain Power in the Eyes of Others
note: Observers rated norm violators, including a person who put their feet on another person’s desk, as more powerful than people who followed the relevant norm.

headline: Can red sneakers make someone look higher status in a formal setting?
title: The Red Sneakers Effect: Inferring Status and Competence from Signals of Nonconformity
note: Across studies, observers sometimes inferred greater status and competence from deliberate departures from dress conventions.

headline: Can the color of a waitress’s shirt change how much she earns in tips?
title: Clothing Color and Tipping: Gentlemen Patrons Give More Tips to Waitresses With Red Clothes
note: The study reported that male diners gave larger tips to waitresses wearing red, with no corresponding increase among female diners.

headline: Can crouching at the table earn a server a bigger tip?
title: Effect of Server Posture on Restaurant Tipping
note: Two restaurant field experiments reported larger tips when servers squatted beside the table instead of standing.

headline: Can singing and moving in time make strangers contribute more to a common pot?
title: Synchrony and Cooperation
note: Groups assigned to activities such as synchronized walking or singing later showed greater cooperation in experimental tasks.

headline: Do infants prefer a puppet that harms a previously antisocial puppet?
title: How Infants and Toddlers React to Antisocial Others
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In puppet displays, older infants’ choices depended on whether the target of a positive or negative action had previously behaved prosocially or antisocially.

headline: Can 15-month-olds track where someone mistakenly expects to find a hidden toy?
title: Do 15-Month-Old Infants Understand False Beliefs?
note: Infants looked longer when an actor reached in a way inconsistent with the location the actor had previously seen. The authors interpreted the pattern as evidence of false-belief understanding.

headline: Can turning up the crunch make the same potato chip taste fresher?
title: The Role of Auditory Cues in Modulating the Perceived Crispness and Staleness of Potato Chips
note: Participants rated chips as crisper and fresher when the sound of their bite was amplified or its high frequencies were boosted.

headline: Can a soundtrack make the same toffee taste more bitter?
title: A Bittersweet Symphony: Systematically Modulating the Taste of Food by Changing the Sonic Properties of the Soundtrack Playing in the Background
note: Participants gave different ratings of the same toffee while listening to soundtracks designed to evoke sweetness or bitterness.

headline: Do people think more abstractly when dressed formally?
title: The Cognitive Consequences of Formal Clothing
note: Across observational and experimental studies, more formal dress was associated with more abstract responses on laboratory tasks.

headline: Can adding a brain scan make the same scientific argument seem stronger?
title: Seeing Is Believing: The Effect of Brain Images on Judgments of Scientific Reasoning
note: Readers gave more favorable ratings to scientific reasoning when summaries were accompanied by brain images than when they had other illustrations or no image.

headline: Can your own phone on the desk lower your score even if you never touch it?
title: Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One’s Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: Participants scored differently on cognitive tasks depending on whether their own phone was on the desk, elsewhere on their person, or in another room.

headline: Can hearing your own phone ring across the room make word puzzles harder?
title: The Extended iSelf: The Impact of iPhone Separation on Cognition, Emotion, and Physiology
note: Participants performed worse on a word search when their own iPhone rang out of reach. The authors also reported higher heart rate and blood pressure.

headline: Can a difference in starting wealth make someone cheat to help or hurt a stranger?
title: Dishonesty in the Name of Equity
note: An initial lottery assigned participants different wealth levels. In subsequent tasks, the researchers reported more dishonest acts that benefited poorer partners or harmed wealthier partners.

headline: Will people defend their choice after a researcher secretly swaps it for the one they rejected?
title: Failure to Detect Mismatches Between Intention and Outcome in a Simple Decision Task
note: Participants picked the more attractive of two faces. Many did not detect when they were handed the face they had rejected and offered reasons for supposedly choosing it.

headline: Will people defend a moral opinion opposite to the one they just marked on a survey?
title: Lifting the Veil of Morality: Choice Blindness and Attitude Reversals on a Self-Transforming Survey
note: Researchers covertly reversed some survey items. Participants often accepted the altered answers as their own and sometimes defended them aloud.

headline: Can people switch which jam or tea they prefer after a researcher secretly swaps the samples?
title: Magic at the Marketplace: Choice Blindness for the Taste of Jam and the Smell of Tea
note: Shoppers sampled jams or smelled teas and stated a preference. Many failed to catch a covert substitution and gave reasons that fit the substituted sample.

headline: Can printed eyes make people less likely to drop a leaflet on the ground?
title: Do Images of ‘Watching Eyes’ Induce Behaviour That Is More Pro-Social or More Normative? A Field Experiment on Littering
note: A campus field experiment reported that printed eyes changed littering rates, with the effect depending on whether other people were nearby.

headline: Can the shape of a glass change how fast people drink the same beer?
title: Glass Shape Influences Consumption Rate for Alcoholic Beverages
note: In the experiment, participants drank a full serving of lager more quickly from a curved glass than from a straight one. The researchers did not find the same pattern for a soft drink.

headline: Can a burst of noise as a racket hits the ball make the shot direction harder to judge?
title: A Preliminary Investigation Regarding the Effect of Tennis Grunting: Does White Noise During a Tennis Shot Have a Negative Impact on Shot Perception?
note: Viewers judged tennis shot direction from videos. An added burst of sound around ball contact led to slower responses and more errors.

headline: Can louder tennis grunts make opponents expect the ball to land farther away?
title: The Sound of Speed: How Grunting Affects Opponents’ Anticipation in Tennis
note: When identical stroke videos were paired with louder grunts, participants predicted deeper landings.

headline: Can a tennis grunt’s pitch tell listeners who is losing the match?
title: Tennis Grunts Communicate Acoustic Cues to Sex and Contest Outcome
note: Players’ grunt pitch differed between matches they won and lost. The authors also reported that listeners could use acoustic cues to judge likely match outcome.

headline: Does smelling sweat collected during fear change how observers react to faces?
title: Titrating the Smell of Fear: Initial Evidence for Dose-Invariant Behavioral, Physiological, and Neural Responses
note: The authors reported measurable responses to sweat collected under fear, with little evidence of a graded response to increasing doses.

headline: Will babies copy an adult who turns on a light with their forehead?
title: Rational Imitation in Preverbal Infants
note: Infants copied an adult’s unusual head action more often when the adult’s hands had been free than when the hands had been visibly occupied.

headline: Will children copy a pointless step even after being warned to ignore silly actions?
title: The Hidden Structure of Overimitation
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Children copied unnecessary steps demonstrated by adults, including under conditions designed to discourage copying irrelevant actions.

headline: Can a different soundtrack change how people rate the same beer?
title: Music Influences Hedonic and Taste Ratings in Beer
note: The researchers reported differences in ratings of the same beer when served with different label and music contexts.

headline: Can a seven-month-old’s gaze follow what somebody else mistakenly expects to see?
title: The Social Sense: Susceptibility to Others’ Beliefs in Human Infants and Adults
note: Infants’ looking times and adults’ object-detection times varied with what an on-screen agent had seen. The authors interpreted this pattern as automatic sensitivity to others’ beliefs.

headline: Will two-year-olds look where someone mistakenly expects to find a toy?
title: Action Anticipation Through Attribution of False Belief by 2-Year-Olds
note: The researchers measured where children looked before an actor could search. The reported gaze bias favored the location consistent with the actor’s outdated information.

headline: Do 13-month-olds expect somebody to search in the wrong place for an object?
title: Attribution of Beliefs by 13-Month-Old Infants
note: Infants watched animated events. Looking times differed depending on whether an agent searched in a location consistent with what it had previously seen.

headline: Can an 18-month-old tell which box a mistaken adult actually needs help opening?
title: Eighteen-Month-Old Infants Show False Belief Understanding in an Active Helping Paradigm
note: Toddlers helped adults with different boxes depending on whether the adult had witnessed a toy being moved.

headline: Will a toddler stop a mistaken adult before the adult reaches into the wrong box?
title: 18-Month-Olds Predict Specific Action Mistakes Through Attribution of False Belief, Not Ignorance, and Intervene Accordingly
note: Toddlers intervened differently when an adult had outdated information about an object’s location than when the adult lacked that information altogether.

headline: Do babies expect an adult to mistake a silent object for a rattling one?
title: Attributing False Beliefs About Non-Obvious Properties at 18 Months
note: The experiments used identical-looking objects with different hidden properties. The authors interpreted differences in looking time as sensitivity to the properties the adult believed the objects had.

headline: Can 18-month-olds infer that a remark corrected an adult’s mistaken belief?
title: Can an Agent’s False Belief Be Corrected by an Appropriate Communication? Psychological Reasoning in 18-Month-Old Infants
note: Infants’ looking patterns differed after a relevant verbal message about an object’s location versus a control message.

headline: Do infants prepare for another person’s reach when it reflects a mistaken belief?
title: Belief-Based Action Prediction in Preverbal Infants
note: The study recorded sensorimotor EEG signals while infants watched an agent. The authors linked changes in those signals to whether the agent was expected to act given what the agent had seen.

headline: Do babies infer who will comfort a distressed puppet from who shared food with it?
title: Early Concepts of Intimacy: Young Humans Use Saliva Sharing to Infer Close Relationships
note: After a puppet became distressed, young participants directed their gaze differently depending on whether a person had previously shared saliva with the puppet or played with it in another way.

headline: Can babies infer who will win a confrontation based on how many allies each side has?
title: Infants Use Relative Numerical Group Size to Infer Social Dominance
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants’ looking times differed when an individual backed by a larger group yielded to a member of a smaller group.

headline: Do babies expect two members of the same group to copy each other’s actions?
title: Preverbal Infants Expect Members of Social Groups to Act Alike
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Looking times differed when animated members of the same group acted differently. The authors interpreted the results as evidence of early expectations about group conformity.

headline: Can eight-month-olds tell which sample of colored balls is unlikely?
title: Intuitive Statistics by 8-Month-Old Infants
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants looked for different durations at samples drawn from boxes containing different proportions of colored balls. The authors interpreted this as sensitivity to sampling probabilities.

headline: Do babies look longer when the least likely animated object exits a container?
title: Intuitions of Probabilities Shape Expectations About the Future at 12 Months and Beyond
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Looking time varied with the number of objects of each kind in a simulated container and which object subsequently exited.

headline: Do babies combine time, location and number to anticipate which object will leave a container?
title: Pure Reasoning in 12-Month-Old Infants as Probabilistic Inference
note: The authors compared infants’ looking times across animated outcomes with predictions from a model incorporating object counts and spatial and temporal details.

headline: Can seconds of silent footage predict students’ evaluations of their teacher?
title: Half a Minute: Predicting Teacher Evaluations From Thin Slices of Nonverbal Behavior and Physical Attractiveness
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Average ratings by strangers viewing brief silent clips correlated with end-of-course teaching evaluations.

headline: Can people pick the intended mental state from a photograph that shows only the eyes?
title: The “Reading the Mind in the Eyes” Test Revised Version: A Study With Normal Adults, and Adults With Asperger Syndrome or High-Functioning Autism
venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
note: Participants selected among four words describing mental states for each photograph. The study reported group differences in how often answers matched the scoring key.

headline: Can a suggestion to see words as meaningless symbols reduce interference from reading them?
title: Hypnotic Suggestion Reduces Conflict in the Human Brain
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: A posthypnotic suggestion reduced color-word interference among highly hypnotizable participants. The authors also reported differences in brain activity.

headline: Does what somebody else can see slow you down when you count visible dots?
title: Seeing It Their Way: Evidence for Rapid and Involuntary Computation of What Other People See
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
note: Participants were slower to report their own view of dots when an on-screen person could see a different number. The authors interpreted the interference as spontaneous perspective taking.

headline: Can someone pass a verbal false-belief test without showing the expected gaze pattern?
title: Mindblind Eyes: An Absence of Spontaneous Theory of Mind in Asperger Syndrome
note: The authors compared adults’ anticipatory gaze during a filmed search task and found a group difference despite success on explicit verbal false-belief tests.

headline: Does guessing what someone is feeling depend on how much the person shows?
title: It Takes Two: The Interpersonal Nature of Empathic Accuracy
note: Viewers inferred how people in recordings felt over time. Accuracy varied with both cues from the person expressing emotion and characteristics of the viewer.

headline: Will a baby help a stranger more after bouncing in time with them?
title: Interpersonal Synchrony Increases Prosocial Behavior in Infants
note: After being bounced in time or out of time with an adult, infants in the synchrony group were more likely to pick up objects the adult dropped.

headline: Do dogs follow human gestures to hidden food better than human-raised wolves?
title: The Domestication of Social Cognition in Dogs
note: The study reported that dogs followed human cues to hidden food more successfully than wolves in its comparisons, and that even young puppies used the cues.

headline: Can great apes choose which box to open for an adult who missed a transfer?
title: Great Apes Distinguish True From False Beliefs in an Interactive Helping Task
note: The apes’ choice of which box to unlock differed depending on whether the experimenter had seen an object being moved. The authors interpreted the pattern as sensitivity to the experimenter’s belief.

headline: Do dogs take forbidden food more often when a person cannot see them?
title: Domestic Dogs (Canis Familiaris) Are Sensitive to the Attentional State of Humans
note: Dogs were forbidden to take food while a person watched or was visually inattentive. Whether they took it and how they approached varied with the person’s visible attention.

headline: Do toddlers prefer a winner who gets their way without force?
title: Toddlers Prefer Those Who Win but Not When They Win by Force
note: Toddlers chose between puppets after watching conflicts. They tended to select a winner when the other puppet yielded and showed a different preference when the winner used force.

headline: Can a familiar accent shape whom a baby reaches toward or whom a child picks as a friend?
title: The Native Language of Social Cognition
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants and children showed preferences for native-language or native-accent speakers on several looking, reaching and choice tasks.

headline: Do babies look longer when two people get unequal shares?
title: Fairness Expectations and Altruistic Sharing in 15-Month-Old Human Infants
note: The authors compared infants’ looking times during equal and unequal food distributions and related their looking patterns to later toy sharing.

headline: Will a hungry toddler give away fruit to an adult who drops it?
title: Altruistic Food Sharing Behavior by Human Infants After a Hunger Manipulation
note: Some toddlers handed the experimenter desirable fruit when the experimenter reached for it, including in a group tested near their usual mealtime.

headline: Do babies expect an animated disc to stop jumping when there is no longer an obstacle?
title: Taking the Intentional Stance at 12 Months of Age
note: Infants watched a disc take a detour over a barrier. When the barrier was removed, their looking times differed depending on whether the disc repeated the detour.

headline: Can one tenth of a second be enough to form a lasting impression of a stranger’s face?
title: First Impressions: Making Up Your Mind After a 100-ms Exposure to a Face
note: Trait ratings after 100 milliseconds of exposure correlated with ratings made without a time limit. The study compared impressions across viewing times.

headline: Can strangers infer someone’s personality from their bedroom or office?
title: A Room With a Cue: Personality Judgments Based on Offices and Bedrooms
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Observers rated room occupants on personality traits. Some ratings agreed with personality measures collected from the occupants or people who knew them.

headline: Can observers estimate personality traits from a single full-body photograph?
title: Personality Judgments Based on Physical Appearance
note: The authors compared impressions from posed and less constrained photographs with personality reports and found that some trait judgments correlated with the reports.

headline: Can remembering a favor make someone wait longer for a larger payment?
title: Gratitude: A Tool for Reducing Economic Impatience
note: Participants asked to recall a gratitude-inducing event made more patient choices between smaller immediate and larger delayed cash payments.

headline: Does remembering a favor make people cheat less on a private coin toss?
title: The Grateful Don’t Cheat: Gratitude as a Fount of Virtue
note: The researchers compared how often participants reported the favorable outcome of a private coin toss after different emotion inductions. The gratitude group reported fewer favorable outcomes.

headline: Can an unused phone on a table make a conversation feel less close?
title: Can You Connect With Me Now? How the Presence of Mobile Communication Technology Influences Face-to-Face Conversation Quality
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
note: Pairs spoke with a phone or a notebook nearby. Some measures of conversational quality and closeness were lower with the phone present, particularly for meaningful conversations.

headline: Can seeing a false headline only once make it seem more accurate the next time?
title: Prior Exposure Increases Perceived Accuracy of Fake News
note: Previously seen fabricated headlines received higher accuracy ratings than unfamiliar ones. The authors examined how plausibility and warnings affected the pattern.

headline: Can feeling angry make people estimate lower risks than feeling afraid?
title: Effects of Fear and Anger on Perceived Risks of Terrorism: A National Field Experiment
note: Participants exposed to fear- or anger-inducing material subsequently gave different estimates of terrorism-related and other risks.

headline: Can a night of sleep help people discover a shortcut they missed while awake?
title: Sleep Inspires Insight
note: After training on a task with a hidden shortcut, participants who slept were more likely to discover the shortcut than groups that stayed awake.

headline: Can a chance to show that you are unbiased make you more willing to express a potentially biased choice?
title: Moral Credentials and the Expression of Prejudice
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants given an opportunity to establish apparently unbiased credentials were more willing to make a subsequent choice that could be interpreted as prejudiced.

headline: Do babies expect a leader to step in when someone takes another person’s share?
title: Infants Expect Leaders to Right Wrongs
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants watched a character take a resource from another. Their looking times depended on whether a third character with a leadership role intervened.

headline: Will an elephant touch a mark on its own head after seeing it in a mirror?
title: Self-Recognition in an Asian Elephant
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: One of three elephants repeatedly touched the visible mark on its own head when a mirror was available.

headline: Does a magpie try to remove a mark it can only see in a mirror?
title: Mirror-Induced Behavior in the Magpie (Pica pica): Evidence of Self-Recognition
note: Some magpies directed more behavior toward a visible mark on their throat when a mirror was present than under comparison conditions.

headline: Do rhesus monkeys know when to skip a memory test?
title: Rhesus Monkeys Know When They Remember
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Monkeys could take a memory test or decline for a smaller reward. They declined more often under conditions associated with weaker memory and tended to answer more accurately on tests they chose to take.

headline: Can telling people a technology is beneficial make its unrelated risks seem lower?
title: The Affect Heuristic in Judgments of Risks and Benefits
note: Manipulating information about a technology’s benefits shifted estimated risks, and manipulating risk information shifted benefit estimates.

headline: Can the car someone drives predict whether they cut off a pedestrian?
title: Higher Social Class Predicts Increased Unethical Behavior
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In a field study, observers coded vehicle status and whether drivers yielded to a pedestrian. The association between the two was used alongside lab comparisons to argue that higher social class predicts more unethical behavior.

headline: Can hearing brief speech change judgments of a job candidate’s social class and starting salary?
title: Evidence for the Reproduction of Social Class in Brief Speech
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Listeners’ class estimates were compared with speakers’ reported class. In a hiring experiment, people with hiring experience formed different competence and salary judgments after hearing brief speech samples.

headline: Can getting left out make a risky bet seem more appealing?
title: Show Me the Honey! Effects of Social Exclusion on Financial Risk-Taking
note: Spending and gambling experiments compared socially excluded and included participants. The authors reported more risk taking in the exclusion condition and interpreted it in terms of the perceived value of money.

headline: Does being left out make people copy a new interaction partner’s movements?
title: I Am Too Just Like You: Nonconscious Mimicry as an Automatic Behavioral Response to Social Exclusion
note: After an inclusion or exclusion manipulation, the researchers counted participants’ mimicry of a partner. Excluded participants copied more in some conditions.

headline: Can a briefly shown face change how quickly people recognize an object as a weapon?
title: Prejudice and Perception: The Role of Automatic and Controlled Processes in Misperceiving a Weapon
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared response times and classification errors for tools and weapons after Black or White face primes, including under a response deadline.

headline: Can a target’s race affect split-second decisions in a video game about armed and unarmed people?
title: The Police Officer’s Dilemma: Using Ethnicity to Disambiguate Potentially Threatening Individuals
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared response times and errors across target race and whether the target held a gun in a simulated decision task.

headline: Can exposure to a Black face change how easily a person recognizes a blurred image related to crime?
title: Seeing Black: Race, Crime, and Visual Processing
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across visual tasks, the researchers compared object recognition and attention after racial or crime-related cues. They interpreted the contrasts as evidence that associations can affect visual processing.

headline: Can a masked tea-brand name sway beverage choice among people who are already thirsty?
title: Beyond Vicary’s Fantasies: The Impact of Subliminal Priming and Brand Choice
note: The authors compared beverage choices or intentions after briefly flashing a brand or a control stimulus. The reported increase in preference depended on thirst.

headline: Can the Russian vocabulary for shades of blue speed up a blue-matching task?
title: Russian Blues Reveal Effects of Language on Color Discrimination
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Russian speakers responded faster to pairs crossing a lexical boundary between blues than to within-category pairs in the study. The advantage was disrupted under verbal interference.

headline: Can speakers of one language name the same odors more consistently than speakers of another?
title: Odors Are Expressible in Language, as Long as You Speak the Right Language
note: The researchers quantified naming agreement for odor and color samples. Jahai speakers used more consistent odor labels than English speakers in the study.

headline: Can oxytocin make people more likely to report a favorable result when their group gets paid?
title: Oxytocin Promotes Group-Serving Dishonesty
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The researchers compared self-reported coin-prediction success under oxytocin and placebo. Higher reported success in the group-payoff condition was interpreted as greater dishonesty.

headline: Can oxytocin make people more willing to spend money defending their own group in a game?
title: The Neuropeptide Oxytocin Regulates Parochial Altruism in Intergroup Conflict Among Humans
note: The researchers compared allocations in intergroup games under oxytocin and placebo, linking differences to in-group cooperation and defensive choices.

headline: Does a person’s social class predict how long their eyes linger on strangers?
title: Social Class and the Motivational Relevance of Other Human Beings: Evidence From Visual Attention
note: Eye-tracking studies compared attention to other people across participants with different measured or reported social class. The authors interpreted the association as a difference in the motivational relevance of others.

headline: Can changing a picture of a defendant change ratings of guilt for the same case?
title: The Influence of a Defendant’s Body Weight on Perceptions of Guilt
note: Participants rated a hypothetical defendant after seeing a photograph. The authors reported that body-weight cues affected guilt ratings in some combinations of observer and defendant gender.

headline: Can one sleepless night increase reports of a detail that appeared only in a misleading account?
title: Sleep Deprivation and False Memories
note: The authors compared false recognition after misinformation across sleep conditions. The effect depended in part on when sleep loss occurred relative to encoding.

headline: Can a partner’s wrong recollection make someone report having seen an object that was never there?
title: Social Contagion of Memory
note: After seeing scenes, participants recalled objects with a partner who sometimes supplied incorrect items. Those suggestions increased later reports of the absent items.

headline: Can seeing an artificially aged image of yourself shift how much you allocate to retirement?
title: Increasing Saving Behavior Through Age-Progressed Renderings of the Future Self
note: Participants exposed to aged or current representations of themselves made different allocations in experimental saving tasks. The authors interpreted the contrasts as an effect of making the future self feel more concrete.

headline: Does copying someone’s posture make the same conversation feel smoother?
title: The Chameleon Effect: The Perception-Behavior Link and Social Interaction
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors counted unintentional movements and compared liking and smoothness ratings between interactions in which a partner did or did not mimic participants.

headline: Can having your movements copied make you more generous toward an unrelated person?
title: Mimicry and Prosocial Behavior
note: The authors compared helping and giving behavior after participants had been mimicked or not, including outcomes directed toward someone other than the mimicker.

headline: Can seeing a picture of one’s partner change pain ratings during a heat task?
title: A Picture’s Worth: Partner Photographs Reduce Experimentally Induced Pain
note: The researchers compared reported pain during thermal stimulation while participants viewed different photographs or received other social cues. Partner photographs were associated with lower reported pain.

headline: Do children say a dead character can still want or know things?
title: The Natural Emergence of Reasoning About the Afterlife as a Developmental Regularity
note: Children answered questions about a dead story character. The authors compared responses about biological and psychological states across age groups and drew conclusions about how afterlife reasoning develops.

headline: Does using a foreign language change how people respond to equivalent gain and loss descriptions?
title: The Foreign-Language Effect: Thinking in a Foreign Tongue Reduces Decision Biases
note: The researchers compared choices made in native and foreign languages in framing and betting tasks. They interpreted some choice differences as reduced decision bias.

headline: Will people build fewer Lego models if each one is dismantled as soon as they finish it?
title: Man’s Search for Meaning: The Case of Legos
note: As piece rates declined, the authors compared how long participants kept building when completed models were retained or immediately dismantled.

headline: Can a person look at the spot where a magician drops an object and still miss the drop?
title: Misdirection in Magic: Implications for the Relationship Between Eye Gaze and Attention
note: The researchers scored detection of a magic method and recorded gaze, comparing overt fixation patterns with whether viewers saw the critical event.
